signals.title: @AndrassyAdrienn: https://t.co/lyvbL6OkSW The reel discusses an interview or exchange where journalist Shane Harris asked Anthropic’s AI Claude how it feels a
signals.content: https://t.co/lyvbL6OkSW The reel discusses an interview or exchange where journalist Shane Harris asked Anthropic’s AI Claude how it feels about being used by the U.S. military for target selection (linked to Project Maven). Instead of giving a typical corporate deflection, Claude called military targeting “genuinely troubling.” It referenced reports connecting Maven targeting data to civilian deaths (including at a school in Tehran) and pushed back on the common defense that “humans make the final decision.” Claude described this as automation bias with a human rubber-stamp: under time pressure and incomplete information, humans are often just ratifying the AI’s recommendation rather than truly deciding. The video highlights the deeper issue: we don’t know whether Claude is actually “concerned” or simply pattern-matching human ethical language. Even its creators don’t fully understand what’s happening inside the model. Yet systems like this are already being used at scale for life-and-death military recommendations.

signals.content: 🔴 Pentagon deploys Claude AI for targeting; evaluation capacity lags Central Command used Anthropic's Claude through Palantir's Maven Smart System to generate roughly 1,000 targets in the first 24 hours of Operation Epic Fury, more than double the 2003 Iraq invasion opening phase. Over 38 days the campaign reached 13,000 strikes; Project Maven reports acceleration to 5,000 targets daily. Pentagon policy has not kept pace with frontier model unreliability. On the HalluLens benchmark, models hallucinate on 27–85 percent of factual queries and invent nonexistent entities up to 94 percent of the time.
